understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call needing their approval, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: By the end of the week the test you feel you are failing is named, and the part of you that can stand in its own worth has the floor.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the pride and the question, and the restless mind between them, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the restless mind comes from needing their approval to settle a clock that is not yours.
week_beats.steady: You hold that praise and blame come and go, and what is yours to do is yours to do.
week_beats.act: You try being on your own side for one evening, letting their praise and their questions come and go without deciding your worth.

understanding.core_struggle: A woman working -hour night shifts and sending money home feels she is failing a test she never agreed to take, because every call ends with when are you getting married.
understanding.mirror: You send them half your salary, and every call ends with the same question you never asked.
understanding.insight: You are building something for them with your work, and the test you feel you are failing is the one they keep asking about.

queries.hook: The pride in their voice and the question at the end of every call, and the restless mind that cannot settle between the two. My parents' expectations weigh on me.
queries.diagnose: When your worth depends on their approval, every word of blame or pressure shakes you; craving approval keeps the mind unsteady.
queries.steady: Praise and blame come and go like the wind; what is yours to do is yours to do, and no one else can take that from you.
queries.act: Practise being on your own side; let their praise and their questions come and go without letting either decide your worth today.
queries.story: A woman who built something for her family with her own hands, faced the same question again and again, and found a way to stand in her own worth.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.for_you: Praise and blame are only words that come and go; your worth rests on your own conduct, not on their opinion.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: Opening verse of 'Advice to the Mind'.
verse.sanskrit: परेषां चेतांसि प्रतिदिवसमाराध्य बहुधा प्रसादं किं नेतुं विशसि हृदय क्लेशकलितम् । प्रसन्ने त्वय्यन्तः स्वयमुदितचिन्तामणिगणो विविक्तः संकल्पः किमभिलषितं पुष्यति न ते ॥
verse.line: Why exhaust yourself daily winning others' approval? Settle inside, and your own clarity grants every wish.
verse.translation: O heart, why do you enter into weariness, day after day trying to please the minds of others in so many ways, to win their favour? When you are at peace within, your own clear resolve rises by itself like a cluster of wish-granting gems: what wish of yours would it not fulfil?
verse.why: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own heart at the start of this poem. He asks why it tires itself out, day after day, trying to win the favor of others. He says the mind replays the past and scripts the future just to please people. The verse proposes that when you settle inside your own peace, your own clear resolve rises naturally. It is like a cluster of wish-granting gems. Once that clarity is there, it fulfills every wish you have.
verse.for_you: The calls with your parents end the same way. Your mind is running a test for their approval while you work your night shifts. The restlessness is not the work. It is the clock you are trying to settle for them. Let your own clarity rise instead.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind rehearses the next call with your parents.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own night shift, trying to please the minds of others.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
verse.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
verse.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from the section on steadfastness. They are telling a person to let the world do what it does. Praise and blame will come. Money will come and go. Death may come today or later. The steadfast person does not step off the right path because of these things.
verse.for_you: You are working the night shift and sending half your pay home. Your parents are proud, and they end every call with marriage. That is their part. Your part is the work you do and the money you send.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment at work when you feel the pressure to prove yourself.
verse.scene_line: You are on your shift, and the call with your parents is still in your ear.
asks: How do I tell their pride from their pressure?
Can I hold the work and the call in the same breath?

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: न हृष्यत्यात्मसंमाने नावमानेन तप्यते / गाङ्गो ह्रद इवाक्षोभ्यो यः स पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Don't swell with praise or burn at a slight; stay deep and still like a river pool.
verse.translation: One who is not elated when honoured, nor pained when slighted, and who stays unruffled like a deep pool of the Ganga, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.for_you: Every call home ends with the same question, and your mind turns it over all night. Praise from them and the pressure to marry are both just weather passing over your work. Your own clarity is the pool. Let the noise of their approval come and go.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when their call does not change the steady focus of your work.
verse.scene_line: You sit in the quiet of your night shift, a river pool untouched by the leaves of their praise and blame.
asks: How do I tell their pride from the test they keep giving me?
Can I stay steady when the next call asks the same question again?
What does my own clarity look like when they are not in the room?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
verse.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.
verse.why: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.
verse.misuse: Not 'stay in the role your family or birth assigned you'. It's about being true to your own nature and calling.

prasang.title: The ignorant and the wise; act free of like and dislike
prasang.summary: Krishna contrasts the attached and the wise, warns that ego claims credit for what nature does, and says to follow your own path rather than imitate another's.
prasang.lesson: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is caught between two armies, unsure of his role and his duty. Krishna tells him that it is better to walk your own path, even if you stumble, than to copy another's walk and pretend it fits. Borrowing a life that is not yours creates a constant fear of being found out. Your own duty, done with your own effort, holds a steadiness that borrowed perfection cannot offer. The wise act without claiming credit for what nature simply does.
verse.for_you: The calls from home are your borrowed path, a life you did not choose but are trying to walk perfectly. Your own shift, your own exhaustion, your own worth are the duty that is truly yours. Let the marriage questions echo in the background like noise.
verse.try_today: Let the next call from home end without you defending your worth.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own duty, imperfect and entirely your own.
asks: What is my own duty when everyone else has a script?
How do I know if I am on the right path?
What does it mean to walk my own path imperfectly?

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
verse.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
verse.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
verse.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu speaks to Nidagha, who is caught in the world of action. Ribhu describes a free person living among others. They let go of what is lost and take up what comes. They do the work at hand and speak gently. Ribhu says this person is busy on the outside but unhurried inside. They are a doer in the world but a non-doer within. They move through life with a clear mind, treating the whole world as family.
verse.for_you: You are working the night shift and sending money home. You are busy on the outside. The call ends with a question about marriage, and your mind stirs. You do not have to decide your worth in that moment.
verse.scene_line: You are busy on the outside and unhurried inside, a doer on the outside and a non-doer within.
asks: How do I let their praise and questions come and go without deciding my worth?
Can I be a doer on the outside and a non-doer within?

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
